$$
y=-2{e}^{u},\,u=-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-2{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m &= 8{e}^{-4x}\big|_{x=- \frac{1}{4}} \\ &= 8{e}^{(-4)\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)} \\ &= 8 e.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}y_1 &= -2{e}^{-4x}\big|_{x=- \frac{1}{4}} \\ &= -2{e}^{(-4)\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)} \\ &= - 2 e.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 &=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(- 2 e) &= (8 e)(x-\left(- \frac{1}{4}\right)) \\ y-(- 2 e) &= 8 e x-(- 2 e) \\ y &= 8 e x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${15}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${72}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${55}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $6$ minutes. Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-15),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-15} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-15} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-15| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-15>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-15 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-15 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-15 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =15+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=72$ and $T(6)=55$:

$$
\begin{aligned}72 & =15+Ke^{-1k} \\ 57 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 55 & =15+Ke^{-6k} \\ 40 & =Ke^{-6k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{40}{57} & =\frac{Ke^{-6k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{40}{57} & =e^{-5k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{40}{57}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=72$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}57 & =Ke^{-1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =57e^{1\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =57\left(\frac{57}{40}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=15+57\left(\frac{57}{40}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =15+(57\left(\frac{57}{40}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 1}=72 \\ T(6) & =15+(57\left(\frac{57}{40}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 6}=55\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${26}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =26 \\ 15+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =26 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =11 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{11}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{11}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{11}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{40}{57} \right)}}{5}}\ln\left(\frac{11}{57\left(\frac{57}{40}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+5\frac{\ln\left(\frac{11}{57}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{40}{57}\right)}≈24\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$
